A cone from a fixed equatorial disk in that ball to a remote superlevel point would have arbitrarily large volume, which rules out unboundedness, including in dimension one.

At radius R beyond the superlevel set, the segment from 0 to any positive f(x) with norm at least R gives f(x) ≤ f(0) exp(−norm(x) log(2)/R). overlap.comparison: This is the compact-support p≥1 inverse-power radial theorem and does not reach the candidate's exponent range. For p≥1 and a log-concave density with interior anchor, take U=int{f>0} and C_j=(1−1/j)(closure(U)∩j times the closed unit ball). These are increasing compact convex neighborhoods of 0 inside U that exhaust U. The continuous restriction truncated to C_j is bounded and upper semicontinuous, and its extended inverse power is exp(−log(f)/(p+1)) on C_j and infinity outside, hence convex. The accepted theorem gives finite convex gauges for those truncations. On each ray from 0 the discarded support boundary consists of at most one point, so monotone convergence of the integrals gives pointwise convergence of the gauges to q_p. Local and exponential bounds give compactness and positive interior for the limit, and the finite convex limit is continuous. This accounts for the p≥1 overlap.

Its radial construction gives the dimension-matched exponent p=r for r≥2, up to dilation by r^(1/r), under an inverse-power hypothesis that includes log-concavity at an interior anchor. Its angular identity and rigidity do not supply the subunit-exponent gauge.
